A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HMF research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, including matching the original proofs across substantial reorganization and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic convergence experiments, video segmentation, email-network prediction and stock-market analysis in Section 6.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthetic, video, stock-market and MovieLens experiments, including repeated-run HMF and HAE results. Some additional MovieLens comparator scores are explicitly quoted from literature.

M1.justification: V1 proposes linear HMF with squared-error fitting. V2 generalizes the objective to other losses, including projected squared error, and introduces heterogeneous autoencoders with shared and source-specific encoders, a common decoder, folded-embedding orthogonality and projection-based training (Section 3.2 and Appendix A). The original linear correction and averaging procedure is retained.

E1.justification: V2 removes the European email-network task from v1 Section 6.3 and adds MovieLens-100K rating prediction. It also introduces incomplete-observation scenarios for synthetic matrices and the roundabout video. The original noiseless synthetic setting and stock-market coverage remain.

E2.justification: The pooled-SVD comparison disappears with the email experiment. V2 evaluates JIVE, RJIVE and perPCA against HMF on synthetic and video data, and matrix completion and Sparse FC on MovieLens. Table 4 additionally includes AutoSVD++, GHRS and GraphRec, explicitly using literature scores rather than newly run comparisons.

E3.justification: The video experiment now removes 40% of pixels, changes local rank from 100 to 30, and evaluates foreground/background MSE and PSNR. New synthetic tests remove 1%, 5%, 10% or 50% of entries, zero-fill comparator inputs and measure subspace error. MovieLens introduces ten genre-based clusters and a 90/10 split of observed ratings evaluated by RMSE.

E4.justification: V2 adds a missing-entry sensitivity study across four masking rates (Table 2) and a t-SNE comparison examining HAE versus standard-autoencoder representations (Figure 4). The email-network topology analysis is removed. These substantially change the robustness and representation analyses, while the original matrix-size convergence analysis and stock case study remain.

E5.justification: V1's eight-seed email results are removed. V2 specifies three seeds for synthetic missing-data tests and 80 seeds for matrix completion, HMF, Sparse FC and HAE on MovieLens. Mean-and-standard-deviation reporting is retained; these counts concern different experiments, not an established increase in runs for a retained experiment.

E6.justification: V1's email errors of 23.6 ± 0.3 for HMF and 24.7 ± 0.3 for pooled SVD disappear. V2 adds missing-data, video and recommendation results: for example, video background MSE is 0.001 for HMF versus 0.021 for perPCA, and MovieLens RMSE is 0.8800 ± 0.0006 for HAE versus 0.8838 ± 0.0006 for Sparse FC. These are new or replaced experiments; the original convergence and stock plots are unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 adds a general-loss KKT and stationarity analysis with an O(1/T) squared-gradient bound, new supporting lemmas and formal Theorem 18 in Appendix D. That formal statement specifies bounded iterates and gradients and beta = 0. The original statistical-error and local-linear-convergence proofs are largely retained in Appendices B–C; v1's appendix Theorem 4 corresponds to v2's Theorem 15.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the contribution from linear shared/unique factor recovery to an extensible framework supporting incomplete observations and nonlinear autoencoders, with recommendation as an explicit application. Identifiability and local squared-error convergence remain central, but the claimed methodological and application scope expands substantially.

C2.justification: V2 interprets genre-aligned HAE embeddings and rating accuracy as evidence that genre-specific features capture useful preference information. It also emphasizes explicit orthogonality enforcement when explaining advantages over earlier decompositions. The stock-crash interpretation and limitations concerning unknown ranks and good initialization remain essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds implementation guidance concerning Sparse FC backbones, AdamW, zero-padded inputs and differentiable folding/projection operations, including Appendix A's PyTorch guidance. V1's RTX 3080 hardware and approximate 0.1-second iteration-time disclosures are removed. Both PDFs link to the same code repository, so code access is not newly introduced.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning relative to JIVE, COBE, RJIVE, SLIDE, iNMF, BIDIFAC and perDL, alongside new recommendation literature. Table 1 explicitly compares distribution, orthogonality, convergence and incomplete-data capabilities. This replaces v1's much narrower discussion centered on conventional factorization and personalized PCA; the personalized-PCA publication update itself concerns the same work.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the separate contribution-summary subsection is absorbed into the narrative. Formulation joins the model section, while misalignment and identifiability move into convergence analysis with substantially shortened explanation. The appendices are reorganized from A–C to A–E, and the author block and author order change.

P2.justification: V2 removes the email table and graph, adds MovieLens results and a t-SNE figure, and introduces related-work, synthetic and video comparison tables. The video display is replaced and enlarged for masked inputs. Algorithm 1 gains client/server color coding and Algorithm 2 is added. Retained convergence and stock figures are relocated within the reformatted document.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's limited comparative validation through relevant decomposition baselines, controlled missing-data tests, quantitative video evaluation and repeated-run recommendation experiments (Tables 2–4). Expanded related work also gives the contribution a better-supported position. These gains outweigh removal of the email study and hardware/timing disclosure. Important qualifications remain: several MovieLens comparisons use literature scores, and the main general-loss theorem does not state the beta = 0 restriction present in its formal appendix version.
